questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go somewhere where I could study in English but still learn a language that I did not know already. I wanted to go to a good university with many interesting Computer Science courses. Lastly, I wanted to go somewhere with mountains as I love to hike and be outside.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I got a lot of information from the coordinators at TUM both from the university overall and from the Informatics Department. I could access TUMonline (like KUnet) as a guest early to browse courses.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Mandatory welcome meeting. MINGA mentor program where you get assigned a mentor who also studies Informatics at TUM - I would really recommend to sign up for this. My mentor was a huge help for me and we ended up becoming good friends.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: There are dorms and I also applied for those but they were not given to Erasmus students this year.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Start looking early as the housing market in Munich is very competitive and expensive. I found both of my apartments on WG-Gesucht (easier if you also know German but most people also understand English). I lived with a friend from Norway. First, we found an apartment for the first two months only and then just counted on finding a new place for the last three months once we were there. It may seem overwhelming at first but it's much easier once you're there and get to know the city and other people.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Registration is done through TUMonline (like KUnet). In my opinion, it's really easy and effective. Most lectures do not have a limit on the number of students - I took a lecture with almost 2,000 students. A really nice thing is that you can sign up for more courses than you need and then deregister later in the semester (often until 1st of July). Exam registration is done separately later.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I asked my mentor for advice on the courses and the professors. The advisors, Anna-Lisa and Martina, from the Informatics Department were also very helpful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful. I got all the classes that I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Apply for Praktikums and Seminars (deadline is early, in February for the summer semester). Take a German language course if you can - you learn German, get to know other international students and it helps balance the workload of 30 ECTS which is a lot at TUM (most people take 20-25 ECTS per semester). Join more courses than you need to and spend the first week attending all of them and figuring out which ones you want to keep.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I found the level comparable to DIKU but it really depends on the courses that you take. Ask your mentor or have a look at the Chair's (forskningssektion) website beforehand to get an impression of what they do and which courses they offer.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Quite similar except for Praktikum and Seminar courses. There are not as many TA sessions, usually only once a week. Covid was very much still a thing so all classes were also streamed/recorded.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Introduction to Deep Learning (I2DL), Master-Praktikum: Machine Learning for Crowd Modeling and Simulation, Seminar - Selected Topics in Machine Learning, German B1.1, Spanish B1.2

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Take a Praktikum and/or a Seminar. You will get more information about those from the Department but they are really interesting, with fewer students and then you also avoid having 6 or more exams at the end of the semester.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None but I was surprised by how expensive housing was.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries are less expensive. Housing is expensive (comparable to Copenhagen or even more expensive).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: ZHS - like KSI/USG at KU. They offer almost any sport and also trips for kayaking, hiking, climbing etc. A really nice way to get to know German students. The classes are mostly taught in German. Weekly language cafés. MINGA mentoring events and day trips. ESNA, the Erasmus network, also arranges events, day trips and weekend trips throughout the semester and during the semester break (before the semester starts).

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: ZHS, MINGA mentoring

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Hiking in the Alps - there are so many opportunities 1-2 hours from Munich. The lakes - Tegernsee, Ammersee, Eibsee, Königsee etc. Take the train to Zürich, Vienna, Salzburg, Verona (and further down in Italy), Prague and other German cities such as Rothenburg, Regensburg, Augsburg, Würzburg etc.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. I found the Germans funny, active, polite and helpful.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Sign up for sports classes at ZHS. Go to beer gardens and festivals.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Very bureaucratic system, most things have to be done physically and on paper. Some people in Bayern are very traditional and conservative from a Danish perspective.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Being outside a lot, hiking, outdoor activities, swimming in the Isar, the chill vibe, Englischer Garten, beer gardens, the proximity to many other nice European cities. So many restaurants and bars.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Spread the workload by taking different kinds of courses - maybe a Seminar, a Praktikum, one or two lectures and a language course. Learn German. Join the MINGA and ESNA events to explore Munich and its surroundings.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: WG-Gesucht for finding apartments/rooms. Some people live in Garching (where the Informatics Department is) but I was really glad that I lived in Munich and just commuted to Garching three times a week for classes. Consider buying a Deutsche Bahn BahnCard if you plan to travel a lot by train. Use the Bayern-ticket when traveling within Bayern. Consider going a month before and taking an intensive German course (either at TUM or at LMU, the other large university).

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know a new city, spending so much time outside and in nature, learning German.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding time for everything.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
